title: When the Undertow Wakes
premise: Marguerite Coldharbour, a bridge inspector whose marriage to Edmund has calcified into routine, discovers a cache of undelivered letters behind her late mother-in-law's wardrobe — letters revealing that Edmund's brother Julian, presumed drowned forty years ago, may have survived and been quietly erased from the family. As Marguerite traces the letters' recipient down the coast, she uncovers a pact of silence made to protect the family name and a fortune built on a lie. When she finally finds Julian alive in a seaside care home, she must choose between preserving the fragile peace Edmund has arranged his whole life around and telling a truth that could shatter it. In the end, the truth surfaces — but Marguerite delivers it on her own terms, dissolving her marriage not in bitterness but in honesty, and finding an unexpected found family in Julian and the woman who loved him in secret.
about_author: Emrys Fairweather is the pen name of a former civil engineer who spent fifteen years inspecting bridges along the Atlantic coast before turning to fiction full-time. Their work explores the quiet architectures of family life, and they live in a converted lighthouse keeper's cottage with two rescue dogs.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On-site at a decaying truss bridge, she measures tolerances with practiced calm while mentally measuring her marriage the same way — everything holding, nothing warm. A perfunctory dinner with Edmund confirms they've become roommates. Emotional beat: the ache of competent loneliness.

chapters.title: The Box Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She opens the box alone: dozens of unsent letters addressed to 'J. Coldharbour,' written in her late mother-in-law Agnes's hand, spanning decades. The earliest is dated three weeks after Julian's drowning. Emotional beat: guilty fascination; she reads one, then another, until 2 a.m.

chapters.title: A Family Arranged Around a Hole
chapters.summary: Alternating Marguerite and Edmund POVs. At Sunday dinner with Edmund's father Gerald, Marguerite watches how the family orbits around Julian's absence without ever naming it. Edmund deflects when she mentions cleaning out Agnes's things. Emotional beat: the eerie choreography of denial.

chapters.title: What Agnes Knew
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with letter excerpts in Agnes's voice. Reading chronologically, Marguerite reconstructs the summer of the drowning: a storm, a boat, two brothers, and a body never recovered. Agnes's early letters grieve; later ones grow strange — hopeful, then accusatory. Emotional beat: dawning suspicion that this was no accident.

chapters.title: Edmund's Silence
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He knows something is wrong; Marguerite has stopped pretending at dinner. Flashbacks to childhood — being told never to ask about Julian, his father's flinty grief. He suspects Marguerite found the box and feels terror, not guilt he can articulate. Emotional beat: a man guarding a door he's afraid to open himself.

chapters.title: The Coast Road
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Claiming a work inspection, she drives to the address from the final letter: a shabby care home in a fishing town called Greyhaven. En route she interviews a retired harbormaster who remembers the storm — and remembers a second boat leaving that night. Emotional beat: the thrill and dread of crossing from curiosity into investigation.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Drowned
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She sees him through a garden window: an old man feeding gulls, with Edmund's hands and Gerald's jaw. She doesn't approach — not yet. Instead she meets Delia Marsh, a local woman in her sixties who visits weekly and bristles at strangers. Emotional beat: vertigo; the dead man breathing sea air.

chapters.title: Delia
chapters.summary: Delia's POV (first time). Over tea in her cottage above the harbor, Delia tells her side: she was seventeen, in love with Julian, pregnant when he vanished. She helped him disappear — because Julian had discovered what Gerald had done with the family shipping money, and staying meant prison or worse. Emotional beat: fierce, weathered loyalty.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, interwoven with more letters. The full shape emerges: Julian took the blame for a financial crime Gerald committed; faking his death was the only escape, and Agnes spent her life paying hush money to keep him safe and silent. Emotional beat: Marguerite recognizes her own marriage in the arrangement — everyone surviving by disappearing a little.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Long Table
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Marguerite confronts Gerald at the family house; Edmund walks in mid-accusation. Gerald neither confirms nor denies — he simply says, 'Your mother chose the family over the truth. So will you.' Edmund says nothing, and that silence wounds Marguerite more than his father's threat. Emotional beat: the marriage cracks audibly.

chapters.title: Tenant, Not Owner
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She moves temporarily into a motel, inspecting bridges by day and rereading letters by night. A tender phone call with her estranged sister reminds her what chosen honesty costs and gives back. Edmund leaves a voicemail that almost apologizes, then doesn't. Emotional beat: grief for the marriage as it might have been.

chapters.title: First Words Across Forty Years
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She returns to Greyhaven openly and sits across from Julian in the garden. He is dry, funny, guarded — a man who rehearsed his own death so long he barely remembers the original role. He assumes she's come as Gerald's emissary. Emotional beat: cautious recognition between strangers who share a face.

chapters.title: What Julian Carried
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. His account of the night of the storm, the forged ledgers, the rowboat, and the decades of watching his family from afar — attending Agnes's funeral disguised as grounds crew. He reveals the cruelest part: Gerald offered him money to stay dead, and he took it, to fund Delia's son's education. Emotional beat: shame entangled with love.

chapters.title: The Son
chapters.summary: Alternating Delia and Marguerite POVs. Delia's son Tom — raised believing his father died at sea — arrives in Greyhaven after Delia, unraveling, lets slip the truth. Tom's fury lands hardest on Julian: forty years of silence, chosen. Emotional beat: found family forming and fracturing in the same hour.

chapters.title: Edmund Comes South
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Unable to bear the silence, Edmund drives to Greyhaven unannounced and sees his brother through the same garden window Marguerite once did. The brothers meet without words at first — two men shaped by the same absence from opposite sides. Emotional beat: grief and relief arriving together, unwelcome guests.

chapters.title: Gerald's Reckoning
chapters.summary: All four Coldharbours plus Delia meet at the Greyhaven inn. Gerald arrives expecting control and finds the story already loose. Confronted with the letters and Julian himself, he finally confesses — not dramatically, but with the flatness of a man reading his own indictment. Emotional beat: the patriarch's power collapsing into mere old age.

chapters.title: The Question the Whole Family Arranged Itself Around
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The central question finally spoken aloud: was protecting the family worth erasing a man? Each character answers differently — Edmund with evasion softening into honesty, Gerald with defiance, Julian with weary yes-and-no, Delia with fury, Tom with silence. Emotional beat: catharsis without resolution; the question matters more than any answer.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A real storm closes in on Greyhaven — mirroring the one forty years ago. Amid preparations, Julian's health fails sharply; the doctor mentions his heart won't survive another winter of secrets or weather. Time, promised by the blurb, is visibly running out. Emotional beat: urgency compressing every unfinished thing.

chapters.title: Where He Died
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, short sections. In the storm's aftermath, the family walks Julian to the cove. Edmund and Julian speak plainly at last — forgiveness partial, real, incomplete. Tom stands beside his father for the first time. Gerald refuses to come, then appears at the cliff path's edge, watching, saying nothing. Emotional beat: mourning a man while he lives.

chapters.title: The Truth, Delivered
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She mails copies of Agnes's letters to the remaining family and to a local historian, ending the pact of silence permanently — her choice, her terms. Gerald cuts her off financially and socially; Edmund, caught between, finally chooses: he asks Marguerite to come home and rebuild. Emotional beat: the cost of survival paid in full, receipt kept.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She and Edmund divorce gently, without villains — two people who were tenants of each other and finally admit it. She takes a permanent post in Greyhaven. Julian, frail but lucid, teaches her to mend nets on Delia's porch; Tom starts calling her cousin, half-joking. Emotional beat: quiet reconstruction, load-tested and sound.

chapters.title: When the Undertow Wakes
chapters.summary: Final chapter, mostly Julian's POV with a closing turn to Marguerite. Julian dies in early spring, at peace, Delia's hand in his, having lived long enough to be known. At the small funeral, the family Gerald once arranged around a hole arranges itself instead around a grave — honestly, imperfectly, together. Marguerite stays after everyone leaves and speaks to the water. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into belonging; the undertow, finally awake, carries nothing away.
